title: How Large Are Human-Capital Externalities? Evidence from Compulsory-Schooling Laws
research_question: How large are the external returns to education at the local (state) level? Specifically, beyond the private wage gain an individual receives from an additional year of schooling, does an increase in the average schooling level of workers in a state raise individual wages, and if so by how much?
data_description: The analysis uses U.S. Census micro-data from the 1950, 1960, 1970, 1980, and 1990 Public Use Microdata Samples (IPUMS), with the baseline sample restricted to U.S.-born white men aged 40-49 (some specifications use men aged 30-39). Key individual variables include highest grade completed (capped at 17), log weekly wages (annual wage and salary income divided by weeks worked), age, quarter of birth, year of birth, state of birth, and state of residence. State-year average schooling is computed from all U.S.-born persons aged 16-64 with positive weeks worked, weighted by weeks worked. The unit of observation is an individual worker. Additional state-level variables describe compulsory attendance and child labor laws (maximum enrollment age, minimum dropout age, required schooling for dropout, minimum work-permit age, and required schooling for a work permit) collected from federal education and labor bulletins covering 1914-1965.
institutional_context: Between roughly 1910 and 1960, U.S. states substantially tightened compulsory attendance laws and child labor laws, together referred to as compulsory schooling laws (CSLs). These laws set maximum ages by which children had to be enrolled, minimum ages at which they could leave school, minimum schooling required before dropping out, and minimum ages and schooling levels required for work permits. Requirements varied widely across states and changed repeatedly over time, with attendance ages rising and work-permit thresholds becoming more restrictive. This period coincided with the high-school movement that Goldin (1998) credits with much of twentieth-century U.S. human-capital growth. Because the laws faced by a child at age 14 were set decades before that child's adult labor-market outcomes, they generated state- and cohort-specific variation in schooling—particularly at the middle- and high-school margins—largely unrelated to later state-level wage shocks.
